prerequisites: Divide a quantity by a time interval.
Convert minutes to seconds and kilometres to metres.
goals: Use SI units and convert lengths, masses, times and speeds.
Calculate average speed and acceleration with consistent signs.
Plot and interpret distance–time and velocity–time graphs.
Find speed or acceleration from gradients and distance from velocity-graph areas.
Plan, evaluate and calculate results from a motion investigation.
Use v² = u² + 2as when acceleration is constant.
Calculate resultants, weight and acceleration; explain stopping and terminal velocity.
Investigate force–extension behaviour and distinguish elasticity from proportionality.
For Paper 2, calculate momentum changes, collisions, moments and support reactions.

sections.title: Quantities, units and conversions
paragraphs: A measurement pairs a number with a unit. In this chapter use kilograms (kg) for mass, metres (m) for distance, seconds (s) for time, metres per second (m/s) for speed and velocity, metres per second squared (m/s²) for acceleration, newtons (N) for force and newtons per kilogram (N/kg) for gravitational field strength.

Convert before substituting into an equation. There are 1000 m in 1 km, 100 cm in 1 m, 1000 g in 1 kg and 60 s in 1 min. To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 1000 then divide by 3600, which is the same as dividing by 3.6. For m/s to km/h, multiply by 3.6.

Unit checks help expose mistakes. Distance divided by time has units m/s; change in velocity divided by time has units m/s². N/kg describes force per kilogram, not mass per unit force. Carry unrounded values through intermediate steps and round the final answer to an appropriate precision for the supplied measurements.

example.question: A toy car has mass 250 g and covers 80 cm in 0.50 s. Express its mass in kg and calculate its average speed in m/s.
example.explanation: The mass conversion is separate from the speed calculation: mass is not required in distance ÷ time.

practice.question: Convert 72 km/h to m/s. How far does an object moving steadily at this speed travel in 3.0 s?
practice.explanation: Convert to m/s because the time is in seconds.

commonMistakes: Using grams in an equation that requires kilograms introduces a factor-of-1000 error.
m/s² means metres per second per second. It does not mean (metres per second) squared.

sections.title: Average speed
paragraphs: Average speed tells you the distance travelled per unit time over a chosen interval. Divide the total distance travelled by the total time taken: average speed = distance ÷ time. Include stops if they occur within the interval described in the question.

Distance is the length of the route travelled; it does not become zero just because an object returns to its starting point. Speed is a scalar quantity. Velocity includes direction, so an object can change velocity by changing direction even when its speed stays constant.

Choose compatible units before substituting. Metres divided by seconds gives metres per second (m/s). To rearrange, multiply speed by time to find distance, or divide distance by speed to find time. A result without its unit leaves the physical quantity incomplete.

example.question: A cyclist travels 540 m, stops briefly, then travels another 360 m. The whole journey, including the stop, takes 150 s. Find the average speed.
steps: Total time for the specified journey = 150 s.
example.explanation: The calculation uses the totals for the same interval. Averaging the speeds of two unequal-duration stages would not generally give the journey’s average speed.

practice.question: A runner covers 1.2 km in 5 minutes. Calculate the average speed in m/s.
practice.answer: 1.2 km = 1200 m and 5 min = 300 s. Average speed = 1200 ÷ 300 = 4.0 m/s.
practice.explanation: Converting both quantities first prevents mixing kilometres and seconds.

sections.title: Reading and drawing distance–time graphs
paragraphs: Put time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis. Label both quantities and units; choose linear scales that use the available space and plot coordinates carefully. Join points according to the model: straight segments for stated steady stages, or a smooth trend for continuously changing motion. A best-fit line need not pass through every noisy experimental reading.

The gradient is change in distance divided by change in time, so it represents speed. A horizontal section means distance is unchanged and the object is stationary. A steeper positive gradient means a greater speed. An upward curve getting steeper represents increasing speed. Read the gradient, rather than the height alone, to compare speeds.

For a straight section choose two well-separated points on the line and calculate (d₂ − d₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). For a curved section, draw a tangent at the required instant and calculate the gradient of that tangent. This gives an estimate of instantaneous speed.

Always read the vertical-axis definition. Total distance travelled cannot decrease. A graph of distance from a fixed point can decrease as the object returns towards that point; the magnitude of that slope describes speed along the line. A displacement–time graph instead has a signed gradient giving velocity.

diagram.alt: Distance-time graph through (0 s, 0 m), (4 s, 8 m), (7 s, 8 m) and (10 s, 20 m).
diagram.caption: The object moves at 2 m/s, rests for 3 s, then moves at 4 m/s. Axes use uniform scales.

example.question: Use the graph to find the speed from 7 s to 10 s and the average speed over the whole 10 s.
steps: Total distance = 20 m; whole elapsed time = 10 s.
example.explanation: The final-stage gradient and whole-journey average describe different intervals. The 3 s stop belongs in the whole elapsed time.

practice.question: A distance–time line rises from (2 s, 3 m) to (8 s, 21 m). Find its gradient and explain what it represents.
practice.answer: Gradient = (21 − 3) ÷ (8 − 2) = 3 m/s. The object travels at a constant speed of 3 m/s over that straight section.
practice.explanation: Subtract both coordinate pairs. Dividing 21 by 8 would ignore the line’s earlier position.

commonMistakes: A high point on the graph is not automatically a high speed. Speed depends on slope.
Do not calculate an area to find speed on a distance–time graph.

sections.title: Plotting motion data
paragraphs: Start with the quantity being plotted. Distance–time and velocity–time graphs can have a similar shape but mean different things. Put time on the horizontal axis; label the vertical axis with either distance or velocity and its unit. A pair (time, value) identifies one point, not a line segment.

Choose uniform scales that fit every supplied value and use a useful part of the grid. For example, if one horizontal square represents 1 s, every horizontal square must represent 1 s. Mark the scales before plotting. An axis label such as velocity / m/s gives both the quantity and the unit.

Plot each coordinate at the intersection of its time and vertical-value readings, then check every point against the table. Join points according to the stated motion. Straight segments are justified for stated constant-speed stages on a distance graph or constant-acceleration stages on a velocity graph. Scattered measurements instead need an appropriate best-fit trend; a table by itself does not prove what happened between readings.

example.question: Two different journeys are modelled in stages. Journey A has distance readings (0 s, 0 m), (4 s, 8 m), (7 s, 8 m), (10 s, 20 m), with constant speed in each interval. Journey B has velocity readings (0 s, 0 m/s), (4 s, 8 m/s), (7 s, 8 m/s), (11 s, 0 m/s), with constant acceleration in each interval. Plot a separate graph for each journey.
steps: For A, label time / s and distance / m. One possible scale is 1 s per horizontal square and 2 m per vertical square, covering 0–10 s and 0–20 m.
Plot A's four coordinate pairs. Join consecutive points by straight lines because the motion within each interval is stated to have constant speed.
A's middle section is horizontal at 8 m: no extra distance is travelled during those 3 s, so the object is at rest.
For B, label time / s and velocity / m/s. A possible scale is 1 s per horizontal square and 1 m/s per vertical square, covering 0–11 s and 0–8 m/s.
Plot B's four coordinate pairs and join consecutive points by straight lines because acceleration is stated to be constant within each interval.
B's middle section is horizontal at 8 m/s: velocity is constant and non-zero, so the object keeps moving.
example.explanation: Compare the finished plots with the distance–time and velocity–time diagrams in this chapter. Both middle sections are horizontal, but the axis quantity changes the interpretation. Other sensible uniform scales are equally valid.

practice.question: Plot velocity against time for (0 s, 0 m/s), (2 s, 6 m/s) and (4 s, 6 m/s), assuming constant acceleration within each interval. Label the axes and explain the two stages.
practice.answer: Use time / s horizontally and velocity / m/s vertically. Plot the three points, draw a straight rising segment from (0, 0) to (2, 6), then a horizontal segment to (4, 6). The object accelerates at 3 m/s² for the first 2 s and then moves at a constant 6 m/s for 2 s.
practice.explanation: The first gradient is (6 − 0)/(2 − 0) = 3 m/s². The second gradient is zero, which means zero acceleration rather than zero velocity.

commonMistakes: Spacing labels unequally while treating the scale as uniform.
Swapping the time and vertical-value coordinates.
Calling every horizontal segment stationary without checking the vertical axis.
Assuming a straight segment or a best-fit curve without considering the stated model and the nature of the data.

sections.title: Practical: investigating a toy car’s motion
paragraphs: A toy car rolling from a fixed release point down a shallow ramp can be used to investigate how its speed changes along the ramp. This is one original example of the specification’s motion investigation, not a compulsory Pearson method. A tennis ball or other everyday object can support a different suitable investigation.

Two light gates connected to a timer can measure the speed at two positions. A card of measured length L attached to the car interrupts each beam. Speed at each gate is approximately L divided by the interruption time; it is an average over the short card passage. Use corresponding events, such as the middle of each interruption, to measure the interval between the two speed readings. Average acceleration is then (v − u) ÷ that interval.

For a simpler stopwatch method, mark a measured length along the track and time the car between the marks. Distance ÷ travel time gives an average speed over that whole region, not the instantaneous speed at one mark. A longer measured interval reduces the percentage effect of a similar reaction-time uncertainty, but may average over more changing motion.

apparatus: Toy car, shallow ramp and secure supports
Metre rule, short rigid interrupt card and two light gates with timer/data logger
Soft stop or catch tray at the bottom
method: Measure the interrupt card length in metres. Fix it so it passes through each beam cleanly.
Set the ramp angle and mark a release point. Position the gates along the track and measure their positions.
Release the car without pushing. Record both interruption times and the time interval between the speed measurements.
Repeat at least three times under the same conditions. Inspect unusual readings, repeat when there is an identified problem and calculate a mean of valid repeats.
Compare speeds at the two positions. To investigate another factor, change only that chosen factor and repeat the measurements.
variables: For a speed-versus-position investigation, the position measured along the ramp is the independent variable and measured speed is the dependent variable.
Keep ramp angle, car, release point, release technique and interrupt card the same. If instead investigating angle, declare angle as the independent variable and hold measurement positions fixed.
safety: Secure the ramp and supports so they cannot slip. Keep feet and loose items away from the run-out.
Use a stop or catch tray; do not use a steep ramp that launches the car off the table.
quality: Electronic timing reduces human reaction-time error; it does not remove card-length uncertainty, alignment errors or variation in release.

Read the ruler square-on to reduce parallax and account for a damaged ruler end or zero offset. Short cards localise the speed measurement but make timing resolution a larger fraction of the interruption time.
Repeat measurements improve confidence in random variation. They do not correct a systematic calibration error. Keep the data and explain any rejected reading.

example.question: A 0.050 m card interrupts the first gate for 0.100 s and the second for 0.040 s. The interval between speed measurements is 0.60 s. Estimate the average acceleration.
steps: Average acceleration = (1.25 − 0.50) ÷ 0.60 = 1.25 m/s², approximately 1.3 m/s² to two significant figures.
example.explanation: The card interruption time gives each gate speed. The 0.60 s interval gives the time between those speeds; it is a different measurement.

practice.question: A student repeats a stopwatch measurement ten times but always starts timing 0.2 s late. Does the mean automatically remove this error? Explain.
practice.answer: No. Repeating can reduce the effect of random differences, but a consistent late start introduces a systematic bias in every reading. Improve or calibrate the timing method.
practice.explanation: Tie the improvement to the source of error instead of saying only “repeat for accuracy”.

sections.title: Acceleration is a rate of change
paragraphs: Acceleration is change in velocity divided by time taken: a = (v − u) ÷ t, where u is initial velocity and v is final velocity. Its SI unit is m/s². An acceleration of 3 m/s² means velocity changes by 3 m/s each second when acceleration is constant.

Choose a positive direction and keep it throughout the calculation. A negative acceleration means acceleration in the negative direction; it does not always mean the object is slowing down. For example, an object moving in the negative direction speeds up if its acceleration is also negative.

example.question: A trolley’s velocity changes from 2 m/s to 14 m/s in the same direction over 4 s. Calculate its average acceleration.
example.explanation: Use the change in velocity, not just the final velocity. The direction is unchanged, so both velocities use the same sign.

practice.question: A cyclist slows from 9 m/s to 3 m/s in 4 s, taking the original direction as positive. Find the acceleration.
practice.explanation: Subtract initial velocity from final velocity; a negative result is consistent with slowing positive motion.

sections.title: Velocity–time graphs and acceleration
paragraphs: Put time in seconds on the horizontal axis and velocity in m/s on the vertical axis. A horizontal line means constant velocity and zero acceleration. A straight sloping line means constant acceleration. A changing gradient means changing acceleration. A point on the time axis has zero velocity at that instant; it need not remain at rest.

The gradient is acceleration: (v₂ − v₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Use a large triangle on a straight line, or a tangent at the required time on a curve. A downward slope has negative acceleration. Whether this slows the object depends on its velocity direction: positive velocity with negative acceleration means slowing, but negative velocity with negative acceleration means speeding up in the negative direction.

Describe each stage with the quantity the axes show. In the example graph the object speeds up uniformly for 4 s, travels at a constant 8 m/s until 7 s, then slows uniformly to rest at 11 s. The middle section is not stationary: it is horizontal above zero velocity.

diagram.alt: Velocity-time graph through (0 s, 0 m/s), (4 s, 8 m/s), (7 s, 8 m/s) and (11 s, 0 m/s).
diagram.caption: Gradient gives acceleration. Area between the line and the time axis gives distance here because velocity is never negative.

example.question: Find the acceleration during the first and last stages in the graph.
example.explanation: The negative result specifies direction. During the last stage velocity remains positive, so its magnitude decreases.

practice.question: An object has velocity −3 m/s, then −9 m/s after 2 s. Find its average acceleration and say whether it speeds up.
practice.answer: a = [−9 − (−3)] ÷ 2 = −3 m/s². Its speed rises from 3 to 9 m/s, so it speeds up in the negative direction.
practice.explanation: A negative acceleration is not always a decrease in speed.

commonMistakes: A horizontal velocity graph above zero means motion at constant velocity, not rest.
A velocity–time graph is not a drawing of the road or the object’s trajectory.

sections.title: Acceleration at one instant: drawing a tangent
paragraphs: A curve has a different gradient at different times. To estimate acceleration at one instant, draw a straight tangent that follows the curve's local direction at that time. Extend it far enough to make a large reading triangle. The triangle's two points must lie on the tangent; they need not lie on the curve.

Read the change in velocity and the change in time from the axes, then divide. Counting squares alone is not enough if the axes use different scales. A line joining two points on the curve gives the average acceleration over that interval, which need not equal the acceleration at your chosen instant.

The original teaching graph below shows a vehicle moving in the positive direction and speeding up more rapidly as time passes. Its tangent at 2 s has a positive gradient. At a horizontal tangent the instantaneous acceleration would be zero, even if the velocity were not zero.

diagram.alt: A curved velocity-time graph rises through (0 s, 0 m/s), (1 s, 0.5 m/s), (2 s, 2 m/s), (3 s, 4.5 m/s) and (4 s, 8 m/s). At 2 s a straight tangent passes through (1 s, 0 m/s) and (4 s, 6 m/s). A dashed triangle uses these tangent points.
diagram.caption: Crimson curve: velocity. Amber straight line: tangent at 2 s. Use the tangent's large triangle, not two convenient points on the curve.

example.question: Use the drawn tangent to estimate the acceleration at 2 s. The two marked tangent points are (1 s, 0 m/s) and (4 s, 6 m/s).
steps: Change in velocity along the tangent = 6 − 0 = 6 m/s.
Time interval for the same triangle = 4 − 1 = 3 s.
Gradient = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s², so the acceleration at 2 s is approximately +2 m/s².

By contrast, joining the curve's endpoints (0 s, 0 m/s) and (4 s, 8 m/s) also happens to give 2 m/s² here. That is the average over 4 s; this numerical coincidence does not make the endpoint method valid for an arbitrary instant.
example.explanation: The supplied tangent defines the worked estimate. A hand-drawn tangent can give a slightly different reading, so show your tangent and triangle rather than quoting unjustified precision.

practice.question: A tangent at 3 s on the same curve passes through (0.5 s, 0 m/s) and (3.5 s, 9 m/s). Find its gradient. Explain why this differs from the average acceleration over 0–4 s.
practice.answer: Gradient = (9 − 0) ÷ (3.5 − 0.5) = +3 m/s². The average over 0–4 s is (8 − 0) ÷ 4 = +2 m/s².
practice.explanation: The curve gets steeper. The tangent describes acceleration at 3 s; the endpoint calculation describes the whole interval. Tangent points may be outside the plotted curve's velocity range.

commonMistakes: Using velocity divided by time from the origin when the tangent does not pass through the origin.
Choosing one triangle point on the curve and the other on the tangent.
Reporting a graph estimate to more precision than the line and scales justify.

sections.title: Distance from the area under a velocity graph
paragraphs: For velocity that remains non-negative, the area between a velocity–time graph and the time axis gives the distance travelled. The units are (m/s) × s = m. Split the region into rectangles, triangles or trapezia and add their areas. A rectangle has area base × height; a triangle has area ½ × base × height; a trapezium has area ½ × (parallel sides added) × separation.

If velocity changes sign, areas above and below the time axis have opposite signs when calculating displacement. Total distance is the sum of the magnitudes of the areas. Split a section at each crossing of the time axis; simply taking the magnitude of the net area can underestimate distance.
For a curved graph, estimate area using strips or counting squares at the required precision. A reading or drawing uncertainty should be reflected in the precision claimed for the final answer.

example.question: Calculate the distance travelled in the velocity graph in the preceding section.
example.explanation: All velocities are non-negative, so adding the three areas gives both distance and forward displacement.

practice.question: An object travels at +4 m/s for 3 s and then at −2 m/s for 5 s. Ignoring the short changeover interval, find its distance and displacement.
practice.answer: Forward area = 12 m; backward area = −10 m. Distance = 12 + 10 = 22 m. Displacement = 12 − 10 = +2 m.
practice.explanation: Distance counts both sections positively; displacement keeps direction.

commonMistakes: Area has units of distance, not acceleration.
Include the factor ½ for a triangle and use the duration of that stage, not its ending time.

sections.title: Estimating distance under a curved velocity graph
paragraphs: When a velocity–time graph curves, a single triangle or trapezium usually does not follow the boundary. Divide the time interval into narrower strips, read each boundary velocity, and approximate each strip by a trapezium. Add the strip areas; each contributes distance in metres when velocity stays non-negative.

Keep the width of each strip in seconds. For one strip, area = ½ × (left velocity + right velocity) × strip duration. Read a shared boundary only once, but use that reading in each of the two neighbouring trapezia.

An estimate is not an exact area. Compare results using narrower strips when the graph allows reliable readings. On this upward-curving graph, straight joins lie above the curve, so these trapezia overestimate its area. Another curve shape can give an underestimate or mixed errors; do not assume the direction of error is universal.

diagram.alt: The same positive velocity curve from 0 to 4 seconds with four shaded trapezia of width 1 second. Boundary velocities are 0, 0.5, 2, 4.5 and 8 metres per second. The straight tops of the trapezia lie above the smooth curve between readings.
diagram.caption: Four 1 s strips give an original worked estimate. The shaded straight-sided strips approximate the curved region; they do not show constant acceleration within each interval.

example.question: Estimate the distance from 0 to 4 s using 1 s trapezia. Readings are 0, 0.5, 2, 4.5 and 8 m/s at times 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 s.
steps: A single 0–4 s trapezium would give ½ × (0 + 8) × 4 = 16 m. It misses much more of the curved boundary.
example.explanation: All velocities are non-negative, so this area estimate gives distance as well as forward displacement. The original readings are supplied exactly for the arithmetic; a real printed graph also introduces reading uncertainty.

practice.question: For 0.5 s strips, supplied velocities at t = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5 and 4 s are 0, 0.125, 0.5, 1.125, 2, 3.125, 4.5, 6.125 and 8 m/s. Estimate the distance and compare it with 11 m. You do not need calculus.
practice.answer: Estimate = 0.5 × [½(0 + 8) + 0.125 + 0.5 + 1.125 + 2 + 3.125 + 4.5 + 6.125] = 10.75 m. This is 0.25 m less than the 1 s-strip estimate.
practice.explanation: Narrower strips follow this smooth curve more closely. Both values are estimates of the curved area, even though their arithmetic uses exact supplied readings.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to multiply by the strip width when it is not 1 s.
Counting a shared boundary as an extra strip instead of part of both adjacent trapezia.
Treating the straight approximation as evidence that the actual motion has constant acceleration.
Using signed net area for total distance when a different graph crosses below zero; split at each crossing and add area magnitudes.

sections.title: Finding speed when time is not given
paragraphs: For straight-line motion with constant acceleration, v² = u² + 2as. Here u is initial velocity, v is final velocity, a is acceleration and s is displacement over the same interval. In a one-direction journey s can be the distance travelled. Use m/s, m/s² and m. The equation is useful when time is not supplied.

List the known quantities with signs before rearranging. To find distance, s = (v² − u²) ÷ (2a). To find acceleration, a = (v² − u²) ÷ (2s). To find the final speed take the positive square root of v²; the equation alone does not determine a final velocity direction after a reversal. Decide direction from the stated motion.

Check the physical conditions. Do not apply one constant-acceleration equation across several stages with different accelerations. A negative value for a computed speed squared usually signals inconsistent data, a sign error or an assumed distance that cannot be reached within that stage.

example.question: A car moves at 12 m/s and accelerates uniformly at 2.0 m/s² over 45 m in the same direction. Find its final speed.
example.explanation: 324 is the speed squared. Taking the square root is essential. The larger final speed agrees with acceleration in the direction of travel.

practice.question: A car brakes uniformly from 20 m/s to rest with acceleration −5.0 m/s². Calculate its braking distance.
practice.explanation: Braking acceleration is negative when forward motion is positive. The resulting distance is positive.

steps: State the applicable relationship and define the interval.
Substitute converted values with consistent signs.
Show the rearrangement and essential numerical working.
Give the requested quantity with units and check physical sense.
answerGuide.caution: This is an original calculation scaffold, not a fixed mark allocation or a validated past-paper template.

commonMistakes: Squaring a speed is different from doubling it.
The equation assumes constant acceleration; it does not describe every arbitrary motion.

sections.title: Forces, scalars and vectors
paragraphs: A force describes an interaction between objects. It can change an object’s speed, direction or shape. Force is a vector: both magnitude and direction matter. Scalar quantities have magnitude only, such as mass, time, distance and speed. Velocity, displacement, acceleration and force are vectors.

Contact forces require contact: normal contact force acts perpendicular to a surface; tension acts along a stretched rope; friction opposes relative sliding or its tendency; drag opposes motion through a fluid. Gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic forces can act without contact. Weight is the gravitational force exerted on a mass. Electrostatic forces act between charges and may attract or repel.

To find a resultant along one straight line, choose a positive direction, add forces in that direction and subtract opposing forces. The resultant is a single force with the same overall effect on this object. Draw arrows from the object, label them and keep arrow length proportional to magnitude when asked for a scale drawing.

Friction dissipates mechanical energy by heating surfaces and their surroundings. In simple sliding situations it opposes the motion. Static friction can provide the forward force that starts a walker or driven wheel moving: identify the surfaces and the relative motion being opposed instead of assuming friction always acts backwards on a travelling object.

Zero resultant force means no acceleration: an object can remain at rest or continue with constant velocity. It does not mean there are no forces. Constant speed around a bend still involves acceleration because the direction of velocity changes.

example.question: A trolley has a 7 N pull to the right and 3 N friction to the left. Find the resultant force.
steps: The resultant is 4 N to the right.
example.explanation: State the direction; 4 N alone does not fully specify a vector.

practice.question: A book rests on a horizontal table. Name its two main vertical forces and explain why it stays at rest.
practice.answer: Weight acts downwards and normal contact force from the table acts upwards. Their magnitudes are equal, so the resultant is zero.
practice.explanation: The forces in this balance act on the same book.

commonMistakes: Mass is a scalar; weight is a force and therefore a vector.
Do not add opposing force magnitudes as if they acted in the same direction.

steps: Choose one direction as positive and record every force along that line with its sign.
Add the signed contributions. Opposite directions subtract; forces acting in the same direction add.
Write the magnitude in N and state a direction. A negative signed result acts opposite to your chosen positive direction.
For the worked example here, 7 N right and 3 N left give 7 − 3 = 4 N right. Magnitude and direction are distinct parts of the answer.
answerGuide.caution: Pearson Physics June 2024 Paper 1P Q5(b)(i), scheme PDF page 8, awards one mark for magnitude and one for direction. This is a source-specific example, not a promise about every force question. The linked generator family remains provisional.

sections.title: Identifying a force and what it changes
paragraphs: Name the interacting objects before naming the force. A falling stone experiences gravitational force from Earth. A charged balloon can attract a nearby object electrostatically without touching it. A hand pushing a trolley supplies a contact force. An object may experience several forces at once; one force's name does not tell you the resultant.

Describe the observable change: speed, direction or shape. A forward resultant can increase a trolley's speed. A sideways resultant can change the direction of a moving object without necessarily changing its speed. Squeezing a stationary sponge changes its shape even when the opposite pushes give no overall translational acceleration.

A scalar describes a magnitude, such as a speed of 5 m/s. A velocity of 5 m/s east also specifies direction and is a vector. Changing from east to north at the same speed changes velocity. Similarly, 4 N upwards and 4 N downwards have equal force magnitudes but are different vectors.

Friction opposes relative sliding, or the tendency to slide, at a contact. For a block sliding right over a fixed floor, friction on the block acts left and can slow it. For a walking person, the shoe tends to push backwards against the ground and the ground's frictional force on the shoe can act forwards. Identify the body and contact rather than memorising 'friction always points backwards'.

example.question: Identify a force and its effect in each case: a stone dropped near Earth; a charged balloon attracting a small piece of paper; a sponge squeezed between two hands; and a block sliding right on a rough stationary floor.
steps: The Earth exerts gravitational force on the stone. With air resistance neglected, the downward resultant increases its downward speed.
The charged balloon interacts electrostatically with the paper. The paper need not carry a net charge for electrostatic attraction; do not infer its net charge from attraction alone.
The hands exert contact forces on the sponge. Opposed pushes can deform it without moving its centre as a whole.
The floor exerts friction on the sliding block to the left. If no other horizontal force acts, this leftward resultant reduces its rightward speed.
example.explanation: Force type, direction and effect answer different questions. Neither an unchanged speed nor an object remaining in place proves that no force acts.

practice.question: A satellite travels at constant speed in a circular orbit. Does its velocity stay constant? Identify the force that changes its motion and say whether contact with Earth is required.
practice.answer: Its velocity changes because its direction changes. Earth's gravitational force acts towards Earth and supplies the inward resultant in this simplified model. The interaction does not require contact.
practice.explanation: Speed is scalar; velocity and force are vectors. Constant speed can coexist with changing velocity.

commonMistakes: Treating unchanged speed as unchanged velocity on a curved path.
Saying opposite forces cannot deform an object because their resultant is zero.
Identifying a force only as 'movement' rather than naming the interaction.

sections.title: Resultant force, mass and weight
paragraphs: For a constant-mass object, resultant force F = ma, where m is mass in kg and a is acceleration in m/s². Use the net force on that object, not automatically the engine thrust or pulling force. The acceleration has the direction of the resultant force. Rearranging gives a = F/m or m = F/a.

Mass measures how much matter an object contains and its resistance to acceleration. Weight is the gravitational force on it: W = mg, where g is gravitational field strength in N/kg. Use the value of g given in the question; do not replace it with an assumed value. Mass is measured in kg and weight in N.

Moving an object to a location with a different gravitational field changes its weight, but does not by itself change its mass. A force balance measures force; a mass quoted from a calibrated scale depends on the relationship between force and local gravitational field strength.

example.question: A 3.0 kg trolley is pulled horizontally with 12 N while friction is 3.0 N. Calculate its acceleration and its weight if g = 9.8 N/kg.
steps: a = 9.0 ÷ 3.0 = 3.0 m/s² in the pulling direction.
example.explanation: The vertical weight does not enter the horizontal resultant when vertical forces balance.

practice.question: An object of mass 5.0 kg is on a planet with g = 4.0 N/kg. Find its weight. A horizontal resultant of 15 N acts on it; find its horizontal acceleration.
practice.answer: Weight = 5.0 × 4.0 = 20 N. Acceleration = 15 ÷ 5.0 = 3.0 m/s².
practice.explanation: Use mass, not weight, in F = ma.

commonMistakes: A force of 12 N is not the resultant if another force opposes it.
An object travelling steadily can have large balanced forces acting on it.

answerGuide.command: Calculate weight from a mass in grams
steps: Identify mass and gravitational field strength; use the value of g stated in your question.
Convert the mass to kg by dividing the gram reading by 1000.
Substitute into W = mg and evaluate; write the result in N.
For an original example, 375 g becomes 0.375 kg. With g = 9.8 N/kg, weight = 0.375 × 9.8 = 3.675 N. Show the conversion and substitution.
answerGuide.caution: The source Q10(a) awards two marks for substitution and evaluation, with one deduction for a clear power-of-ten mass conversion error. Its permitted choices of g are specific to that source. This new generator explicitly states g and remains experimental; its marking is not yet calibrated.

sections.title: Choosing and rearranging force equations
paragraphs: First identify the requested quantity. In F = ma, F is the resultant force on the chosen object along the chosen direction. In W = mg, W is specifically the gravitational force. The same object may have a weight, a pulling force and a frictional force; do not substitute whichever number happens to be labelled 'force'.

Useful rearrangements are m = F/a and a = F/m, or m = W/g and g = W/m. Keep the units alongside the numbers: mass in kg, resultant and weight in N, acceleration in m/s², and gravitational field strength in N/kg. Convert a mass stated in grams before using either relationship.

Check that an inverse calculation is determined. If both resultant force and acceleration are zero, F = ma does not determine the mass: every mass is consistent with that balance. Dividing zero by zero is not a mass measurement. Use a non-zero acceleration to infer mass from F/a.

The signs of resultant force and acceleration must agree when one axis convention is used and mass is positive. A negative acceleration may slow a positive-moving object or speed a negative-moving object; it does not imply negative mass.

example.question: A trolley is pulled right with 21 N against 6 N friction to the left. Its acceleration is 2.5 m/s² to the right. Find its mass and its weight where g = 9.8 N/kg. Vertical forces balance.
steps: Take right as positive. Horizontal resultant F = 21 − 6 = 15 N.
Rearrange F = ma to m = F/a.
Now use the gravitational relationship: W = mg = 6.0 × 9.8 = 58.8 N, downwards.
The 21 N pull is not the resultant, and the vertical weight is not part of this horizontal force balance.
example.explanation: The first calculation finds mass from horizontal acceleration; the second uses that mass to find a different force.

practice.question: An object weighs 36 N where g = 3.0 N/kg. A horizontal resultant of 9.0 N then acts on it while its vertical forces balance. Find its mass and horizontal acceleration.
practice.answer: m = W/g = 36 ÷ 3.0 = 12 kg. a = F/m = 9.0 ÷ 12 = 0.75 m/s² in the direction of the horizontal resultant.
practice.explanation: Use the same mass in both relationships. Substituting the 36 N weight as the horizontal resultant would describe a different force balance.

commonMistakes: Finding mass from a single applied force while ignoring opposition.
Using weight in N where the relationship requires mass in kg.
Assuming F/a determines mass when both F and a are zero.

sections.title: Thinking distance, braking distance and stopping distance
paragraphs: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Thinking distance is the distance travelled between detecting a hazard and beginning to brake. Braking distance is the distance travelled after braking starts until the vehicle stops.

If speed is approximately constant during reaction time, thinking distance = initial speed × reaction time. Greater speed or longer reaction time increases thinking distance. Tiredness, alcohol, some drugs and distraction can lengthen reaction time; state the link from reaction time to extra distance travelled before braking.

Braking depends on initial speed and the available retarding force. For constant braking acceleration magnitude, braking distance = u²/(2|a|). Doubling speed then quadruples braking distance, whereas thinking distance only doubles if reaction time is unchanged. The squared relationship assumes the same deceleration and is not a universal claim about changing roads or braking systems.

Wet or icy surfaces and worn tyres can reduce the available friction with the road. For the same initial speed, less retarding force gives smaller deceleration and a longer braking distance. Poor brakes can also reduce retarding force. A greater mass gives smaller deceleration for the same braking force, increasing braking distance. Do not assume that force stays fixed in every real comparison: specify the conditions.

example.question: A driver travels at 20 m/s, reacts in 0.75 s and then brakes at a constant 5.0 m/s² until rest. Find the stopping distance.
example.explanation: The two distances correspond to different stages and must be calculated separately.

practice.question: At the same speed and under the same braking conditions, reaction time rises from 0.60 s to 0.90 s. Speed is 15 m/s. How much further does the car travel before stopping?
practice.answer: Extra thinking distance = 15 × (0.90 − 0.60) = 4.5 m. Braking distance is unchanged under the stated conditions, so stopping distance increases by 4.5 m.
practice.explanation: A reaction-time change affects the thinking stage; it does not automatically change braking force.

commonMistakes: “Bad weather increases stopping distance” needs a mechanism: reduced friction, smaller deceleration, longer braking distance.
Do not confuse the time needed to stop with the distance travelled while stopping.

sections.title: Falling objects and terminal velocity
paragraphs: Consider an object released from rest and falling vertically through air. Weight acts downwards. Drag acts upwards and generally grows as speed increases. Initially drag is small, so there is a downward resultant and the object accelerates downwards.

As speed increases, drag increases. The downward resultant becomes smaller, so acceleration decreases. Eventually drag balances weight. Resultant force and acceleration are then zero, but the object continues falling at a constant terminal velocity.

Opening a parachute greatly increases drag at the current speed. Drag can initially exceed weight, giving an upward resultant while the person is still moving downwards, so the person slows down. As downward speed falls, drag reduces until it again equals weight. The new terminal speed is lower. Weight is approximately unchanged during this short interval.

In a vacuum there is no air resistance. Near a planet’s surface, neglecting changes in g, falling objects accelerate under gravity and do not acquire a drag-limited terminal velocity. For a real falling object there can also be buoyancy; the usual simplified school model neglects it compared with weight.

example.question: A falling object weighs 60 N and has upward drag of 42 N. Its mass is 6.0 kg. Find the resultant and acceleration, taking down as positive.
example.explanation: Drag has reduced acceleration below the value obtained from weight alone.

practice.question: A skydiver falls at constant velocity. Is the resultant force zero? Does this mean the weight is zero?
practice.answer: The resultant is zero because upward drag balances downward weight. Weight is not zero; the two forces cancel in the resultant.
practice.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, not absence of force.

commonMistakes: Terminal velocity is a speed state, not the name of a force.
If a parachute opens, the person does not instantly move upwards; upward acceleration first reduces downward velocity.

sections.title: Practical: force, extension and elastic behaviour
paragraphs: Extension is stretched length minus original length. Elastic behaviour means an object regains its original shape when the deforming forces are removed. Permanent deformation means it does not fully recover. Elastic behaviour and proportional behaviour are different: a material can recover its shape even if its force–extension graph is curved.

In a Hooke’s-law region, force is proportional to extension: doubling force doubles extension. A force-on-vertical-axis graph is a straight line through the origin in this region. Its gradient gives stiffness, often written k in F = kx. Beyond the limit of proportionality the graph stops being linear. The elastic limit describes recovery after unloading; these limits should not be assumed identical.

Compare a helical spring, metal wire and rubber band using appropriate safe loads and length measurements. Do not presume all three have the same graph. Many springs and wires show an approximately linear region, while a rubber band can show pronounced non-linearity and a different unloading path. Use the measured data to describe each material.

Metal wire extensions can be very small. A long wire, a suitable pointer/scale or a displacement sensor can make extension easier to resolve. Different materials and dimensions need different safe load ranges; a meaningful comparison must state what dimensions and conditions are controlled.

example.question: A spring is 12.0 cm long without a load and 15.5 cm long with a 2.0 N load in its linear region. Find extension and stiffness.
example.explanation: Stiffness uses extension, not total length.

practice.question: A stretched rubber band follows a curved force–extension graph but returns to its starting length after unloading. Is its behaviour elastic? Must it obey Hooke’s law throughout?
practice.answer: It is elastic over this loading cycle because it returns to its original length. It does not obey Hooke’s law throughout the curved region because force is not proportional to extension.
practice.explanation: Recovery and proportionality are distinct properties.

commonMistakes: Measure extension from the unloaded reference length, not from zero on the ruler.
A straight segment that does not pass through the physically appropriate origin does not by itself demonstrate direct proportionality.

apparatus: Secure clamp stand, boss and clamp; helical spring, suitable wire or rubber band
Mass hanger with small known masses, ruler and pointer or displacement sensor
method: Record the specimen’s length before attaching the load, using fixed reference points. When finding total applied force, include the mass of the hanger as well as the added masses.
Add loads in small steps, allowing motion to settle before reading length at eye level.
Calculate force from total load mass using W = mg and calculate extension from the reference length.
Record repeat readings and plot force against extension with labelled units. Identify where a straight proportional region ends.
Unload in steps and compare the final length with the original. Repeat for other materials within their safe ranges.
variables: Independent variable: applied force. Dependent variable: extension.
For a repeat test keep the same specimen, initial gauge length, temperature, support arrangement and reading method. State any change when comparing different materials or dimensions.
safety: Secure or weight the stand against tipping. Keep loads over a catch tray and away from feet.
Wear eye protection because a stretched specimen may snap. Use a screen where appropriate and do not exceed the safe load of the apparatus.
quality: Use a pointer close to the ruler and read perpendicular to it to reduce parallax. Record original length and final length with the same reference points.
A sensor or longer gauge length can improve resolution for small wire extensions. Repeats reveal scatter but do not fix a zero error.
Inspect unloading recovery before claiming elastic behaviour; a loading graph alone does not demonstrate recovery.

If a small preload is needed to straighten a wire, record it explicitly. Length changes measured from this preloaded position correspond to additional force above the preload, not automatically to total force from zero. Keep the force and extension reference states consistent.

diagram.caption: An illustrative proportional region. Gradient = 2 N/cm = 200 N/m. These data describe a different spring from the calculation below.

sections.title: Paper 2: momentum and conservation
paragraphs: Momentum p = mv, where mass is in kg and velocity in m/s, giving kg m/s. Momentum is a vector. Choose one positive direction for all objects in a calculation. Two equally fast objects can have opposite momenta if their directions differ.

The total momentum of a system is conserved if no resultant external force acts on it. During a short collision, outside forces may sometimes be neglected compared with the interaction forces; state this approximation. Add all momenta before and equate them to all momenta after.

For two objects that stick together, they share a final velocity: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v. For objects that separate, keep separate final velocities. Conservation of momentum does not imply that kinetic energy is conserved: in an inelastic collision kinetic energy can transfer to internal energy, deformation and sound.

Recoil uses the same rule. If the system is initially at rest, its total momentum is zero. The two parts then move with equal-magnitude, opposite-direction momenta, but not necessarily equal speeds if their masses differ.

example.question: A 0.60 kg trolley moving right at 2.0 m/s hits a stationary 0.40 kg trolley. They stick together. Find the final velocity, neglecting external horizontal forces.
steps: Initial total momentum = 0.60 × 2.0 + 0.40 × 0 = 1.2 kg m/s to the right.
example.explanation: The mass after sticking is the total mass, and momentum is conserved for the two-trolley system.

practice.question: A 2.0 kg object moves right at 3.0 m/s and sticks to a 1.0 kg object moving left at 2.0 m/s. Find their common velocity, neglecting external horizontal forces during the collision.
practice.answer: Taking right as positive: momentum = 2.0 × 3.0 + 1.0 × (−2.0) = 4.0 kg m/s. Common velocity = 4.0 ÷ 3.0 = 1.33 m/s to the right.
practice.explanation: Opposing momenta subtract. The more massive object’s direction is not sufficient by itself; compare momenta.

commonMistakes: Do not conserve the momentum of only one trolley while it interacts with another; choose the whole system.
Momentum conservation does not mean each object keeps its own momentum.

sections.title: Paper 2: finding mass and recoil from momentum
paragraphs: Conservation can find an unknown mass, velocity or momentum. First draw the complete interacting system and choose a positive direction. Write total momentum before = total momentum after, retaining the unknown wherever that same object occurs.

For a moving trolley that sticks to a stationary trolley, the unknown mass may appear on both sides of the equation. Collect those terms before dividing. A sticking collision cannot make their common speed exceed the original moving trolley’s speed when the other trolley starts at rest and external forces are negligible.

To find a missing final momentum, subtract the other final momenta from the conserved total. For two initially stationary objects that push apart, total momentum remains zero if external forces are negligible. Their momenta are opposite, while their speeds depend on their masses.

example.question: A trolley of unknown mass m travels right at 3.0 m/s and sticks to a stationary 0.80 kg trolley. Their common velocity is 1.0 m/s right. Find m, neglecting external horizontal forces.
example.explanation: The moving trolley contributes to the combined mass after the collision, so omitting m on the right would give the wrong answer.

practice.question: Two trolleys, of masses 0.60 kg and 0.90 kg, start at rest and push apart. The 0.60 kg trolley travels right at 1.5 m/s. Neglect external horizontal forces. Find the other trolley’s momentum and velocity.
practice.answer: Taking right as positive, the first momentum is +0.90 kg m/s. The second must be −0.90 kg m/s so the total stays zero. Its velocity is −0.90 ÷ 0.90 = −1.0 m/s, meaning 1.0 m/s left.
practice.explanation: Equal and opposite momenta do not mean equal speeds. The heavier trolley moves more slowly.

commonMistakes: Do not drop an unknown mass from the final combined mass.
For recoil, zero total momentum does not mean each trolley has zero momentum.
Check the total momentum using your calculated answer; do not check only the final speed.

sections.title: Paper 2: force, stopping time and safety
paragraphs: Average resultant force equals change in momentum divided by the time taken: F = (mv − mu)/t for constant mass. Keep velocity signs. This is the average force over the interval; an impact force can vary greatly during that time.

For the same mass and initial and final velocities, the momentum change is fixed. Increasing the stopping time reduces the average force. Crumple zones deform, extending the stopping interval while dissipating energy. Seat belts restrain occupants and can stretch in a controlled way; airbags cushion contact and extend the interval over which an occupant comes to rest.

Airbags and belts can also spread contact force over a larger area, reducing pressure on the body. Keep this distinct from the time–momentum explanation of force reduction. A safety feature does not remove the requirement to change momentum; it changes how that change occurs.

example.question: A 60 kg passenger moving at 10 m/s comes to rest. Compare average force magnitudes for stopping times of 0.10 s and 0.50 s.
example.explanation: The same momentum change occurs over five times longer, so the average force magnitude is one fifth as large.

practice.question: Explain why “an airbag reduces momentum” is an incomplete safety explanation.
practice.answer: The passenger’s momentum must fall to zero with or without the airbag in the stated stop. The airbag increases stopping time; for the same change in momentum, average force is smaller.
practice.explanation: State the fixed quantity, the changed quantity and their relationship.

commonMistakes: Do not say the force is zero because the passenger is eventually at rest.
Do not mix up a reduced force with a reduced momentum change when comparing identical starting and ending velocities.

sections.title: Paper 2: force during a rebound
paragraphs: A reversal of direction changes the sign of velocity. The change is final momentum minus initial momentum, not the difference between two unsigned speeds. Choose the positive direction before substituting into F = (mv − mu)/t.

The calculated force is the average resultant force on the chosen object over the stated interval. To identify it with a particular contact force, other forces in that direction must be negligible or included separately.

The same relation can find time: t = (mv − mu)/F, using consistent signs. Alternatively, divide the magnitude of the momentum change by the magnitude of the corresponding average force. A negative calculated time indicates inconsistent signs or an impossible stated model.

example.question: A 0.20 kg ball travels horizontally right at 6.0 m/s, hits a vertical wall and rebounds left at 4.0 m/s. Contact lasts 0.050 s. Find the average horizontal resultant force on the ball.
steps: Take right as positive: u = +6.0 m/s and v = −4.0 m/s.
Average force = −2.0 ÷ 0.050 = −40 N: 40 N to the left.
example.explanation: Subtracting the speeds as 6.0 − 4.0 would miss the reversal. If other horizontal forces are negligible, this is also the average horizontal force from the wall.

practice.question: For the same ball and the same initial and final velocities, the average horizontal resultant force is instead 25 N left. Find the contact time.
practice.explanation: The momentum change is unchanged. A smaller average force magnitude requires a longer interval.

commonMistakes: A rebound requires opposite signs for the incoming and outgoing velocities.
State which object experiences the force: the force on the wall is the opposite member of the interaction pair.
Average force is not necessarily the maximum force during contact.

sections.title: Paper 2: Newton’s third law
paragraphs: When object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal-magnitude force of the same type in the opposite direction on object A. The pair acts at the same time and on different objects. Neither force needs to wait for the other.

For example, a hand pushes a wall and the wall pushes the hand with an equal and opposite contact force. Earth pulls a falling ball gravitationally and the ball pulls Earth gravitationally. The forces are equal, but the accelerations can differ enormously because the masses differ.

Third-law pairs do not cancel in the force equation for one object because only one force of the pair acts on that object. A book’s weight and the table’s upward force can balance on the book, but they are not a third-law pair: they have different interaction partners and both act on the book.

example.question: A skater pushes another skater with 40 N. The skaters have masses 50 kg and 80 kg. Ignoring other horizontal forces, compare force magnitudes and accelerations.
steps: Each skater experiences a 40 N force, in opposite directions.
example.explanation: Equal forces do not imply equal accelerations when masses differ.

practice.question: What is the third-law partner to Earth’s gravitational force on a book?
practice.answer: The book’s gravitational force on Earth, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
practice.explanation: It is not the table’s contact force on the book.

commonMistakes: Specify both objects in each force description.
The action and reaction act on different objects, so they do not cancel in a single-object force diagram.

sections.title: Paper 2: moments and centre of gravity
paragraphs: The moment of a force about a pivot measures its turning effect: moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action. Use N and m to obtain N m. The relevant distance is the shortest perpendicular distance, not automatically the length of the lever.

Choose clockwise or anticlockwise for each force’s turning effect. A force whose line of action passes through the pivot has zero moment about that pivot. A larger force or perpendicular distance produces a larger moment.

An object’s weight can be treated as acting through its centre of gravity. For a uniform symmetrical object in a uniform gravitational field this is at its geometric centre; do not assume that for a non-uniform object.

For rotational equilibrium, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment about the same pivot. For an object also not accelerating linearly, resultant force must be zero. Balancing moments alone is not the complete condition for translational and rotational equilibrium.

example.question: A light beam pivots at its centre. A 12 N force acts downwards 0.25 m to the left of the pivot. What downward force 0.15 m to the right balances it?
example.explanation: The beam is light, so its own weight is neglected. Both forces are perpendicular to the horizontal beam.

practice.question: A force of 8 N has a line of action at a perpendicular distance of 0.30 m from a pivot. Find the moment. What happens if its line of action moves through the pivot?
practice.answer: Moment = 8 × 0.30 = 2.4 N m. If the line of action passes through the pivot, the perpendicular distance is zero and the moment is zero.
practice.explanation: Force can remain non-zero even when its moment about a particular pivot is zero.

commonMistakes: The unit for a moment is N m, not N/m.
If a heavy beam’s own weight matters, include it acting at the centre of gravity.

sections.title: Paper 2: loads on a beam supported at both ends
paragraphs: A light beam has negligible weight compared with the applied load. Consider a horizontal beam of length L supported at both ends, with a downward load W at distance x from its left end. In static equilibrium, the upward reactions satisfy R_left + R_right = W.

Take moments about the left end: R_right × L = W × x. The left reaction has no moment about that end. Therefore R_right = Wx/L and R_left = W − R_right. Moving the load towards the right increases the right reaction and decreases the left reaction, while their sum remains W.

For a centred load the reactions are equal. At an end, the reaction at that end carries the whole load in the ideal model. If the beam has appreciable weight, include its weight at its centre of gravity. If a load moves beyond the supports, the assumption that both simple supports can supply the required reactions must be re-examined.

example.question: A light 2.0 m beam carries a 100 N load 0.50 m from the left support. Find both support reactions.
steps: Vertical force balance: R_left = 100 − 25 = 75 N upwards.
example.explanation: The support nearer the load carries more force. The two reactions add to 100 N.

practice.question: Move the same 100 N load to 1.50 m from the left end of the 2.0 m beam. Find both reactions.
practice.explanation: Moving towards the right transfers load to the right support.

commonMistakes: Do not assume each support carries half the load when the load is off-centre.
Take all moments about the same chosen point, using the correct distance for each force.

diagram.alt: Light 2.0 m beam with a 100 N load 0.50 m from the left support, and upward reactions of 75 N on the left and 25 N on the right.
diagram.caption: Force balance: 75 + 25 = 100 N. Moments about the left support: 25 × 2.0 = 100 × 0.50 = 50 N m. Arrows show directions; they are not a force scale drawing.
